alt: Units 1 and 2 make up the International AS; the full A-level adds Units 3 to 5 on development, environment and technology. Unit 2 has 60 marks: Section A on socialisation and social control (40 marks) and Section B on research methods and theory (20 marks).
caption: Unit 2 completes the International AS and is split 40:20 between two sections.

alt: Five numbered sub-sections of 3.1.2: individuals and society, socialisation, social identities and social change, social control, and deviance, harm and crime, plus the six named sociologists for Unit 2.
caption: Deviance, harm and crime is a full sub-section, not a footnote.

alt: Formal social control through government, police and courts is compared with informal control through families, schools, peers, media, religion and work. Key concepts are stigma and othering, Althusser’s state apparatuses and interpellation, and Gramsci’s hegemony.
caption: Control can be formal or informal, and every agency uses sanctions.

alt: The content of 3.1.2.5: the social construction of crime and deviance, eight named crime types, social harms that are not crimes, three ways of measuring crime, and patterns by gender, class, age and ethnicity.
caption: Crime is socially constructed, measured in several ways and unevenly distributed.

alt: Positivists favour quantifiable methods such as questionnaires and official statistics to find patterns; interpretivists favour unstructured interviews and participant observation to capture meaning. Triangulation combines the two.
caption: Strong answers recognise that triangulation can combine both traditions.

after: ## Worked example: applying theory to method choice
alt: Positivist and interpretivist approaches to working-class underachievement compared: official statistics show broad patterns but not causes, while interviews and observation reveal experience but are hard to generalise.
caption: Justify the method choice theoretically, not only practically.
